claims.text: Ti2VZrNb0.5Al0.5 is a lightweight multi-principal-element alloy composition.
The Ti2VZrNb0.5Al0.5 precursors are initially in a disordered solid-solution state.
A thermal shock near 1100 K for tens of milliseconds can form multi-principal-element nanoparticles.
Reheating near 1100 K for about 5 minutes induces a disorder-to-order transition in Ti2VZrNb0.5Al0.5.
Rapid cooling near 10^4 K/s locks in the ordered structure.
The processing route produces an ordered intermetallic phase with an L10 structure.
The processed alloy has a natural composite microstructure containing non-transforming heterogeneities.
The disorder-to-order transition produces a long-range-order parameter approaching 100%.
The transition forms stable intermetallic nanoparticles that resist phase separation.
The cocktail effect and a strain-glass transition enhance mechanical strength and oxidation resistance.
The processed alloy will have hardness greater than 1.5 GPa.
The processed alloy will have a density of approximately 6.5 g/cm3.
The alloy will show minimal oxidation weight gain after 100 hours at 1000 degrees Celsius.
The alloy will have a corrosion current density below 0.1 microampere per square centimeter in 3.5 wt.% NaCl.
Traditional annealing at 1100 K for 3 hours typically causes phase separation.
Traditional annealing produces lower hardness and oxidation resistance than the proposed rapid-processing route.
Particles must be smaller than 60 nm to achieve full ordering.
The processing temperature must remain between 1050 and 1150 K.
The cooling rate must exceed 10^3 K/s to prevent phase separation.
Inferior performance from the traditionally annealed control would falsify the proposed rapid-processing hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that rapid processing outperforms traditional annealing, but the proposed falsification rule says that observing poorer hardness, corrosion resistance, or oxidation resistance in the traditional control would falsify the hypothesis. Those observations would instead support the predicted superiority of rapid processing. Falsification would require the rapid-processed material to fail its thresholds or to show no advantage over the control.
